| 2026-07-27 (session) | `agent-portal-extended-token-refresh-403-fix-2026-07-27` | claude-code | dev+docs+review | User reported the just-shipped `v0.2.5` token-refresh fix wasn't actually working ("not automatically refresh... I should go back and come"). Investigated instead of assuming the fix was sound: re-tested against the live server with `curl` and found the real cause — this backend's Spring Security returns **403** for every auth failure (no token, invalid token, unauthenticated WebSocket handshake), **never 401**, confirmed on both `/api/**` and `/ws/websocket`. `v0.2.5`'s fix used OkHttp's `Authenticator`, which only auto-fires on 401 — it was correct, reviewed, shipped, and never once executed. Rebuilt properly: extracted the refresh call into `TokenRefresher.kt`, made the REST-side trigger a plain `Interceptor` (sees every status code) that retries on 403, and added explicit retry-on-403 logic directly in `StompWebSocketClient.connect()` since a WebSocket upgrade doesn't go through interceptor retry the same way. Verified all three legs against the live server before writing Kotlin (valid-token handshake → 101, no-token handshake → 403, refresh endpoint → 200) — then hired a Reviewer explicitly instructed not to repeat the previous review's blind spot (verify the trigger condition really fires, not just that the logic is internally correct). That reviewer independently re-confirmed the 403 diagnosis with its own curl tests, but caught a genuine NEW bug: the WebSocket retry's recursive call hit its own reentrancy guard (state still `CONNECTING`, never reset) and would have silently stuck forever — the same "stops working, no error" symptom, shipped a different way. **NO-GO.** Fixed (reset state to `DISCONNECTED` before the retry call), re-reviewed by a fresh reviewer instructed to trace the full retry sequence end-to-end rather than assume the fix was sufficient — **GO**, confirmed the sequence always terminates in `CONNECTED` or `FAILED`, confirmed `gradlew assembleDebug`/`lintDebug` directly rather than trusting the commit message.
